title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #878: Unconventional Number Theoretic Functions**

Define f(n) = ∑ pᵢ^ℓᵢ where ℓᵢ = ⌊log_{pᵢ} n⌋, and F(n) = max ∑ aᵢ over coprime decompositions.

**Four Open Questions:**
1. Is f(n) = o(n log log n) for almost all n, while F(n) ≫ n log log n?
2. Is max_{n≤x} f(n) ~ x log x / log log x?
3. Do max f and max F coincide?
4. What is the asymptotic of H(x) = ∑ f(n)/n?
mathContext: These functions are 'unconventional' because the summand p^ℓ depends on the whole number n (through ℓ = ⌊log_p n⌋), not just on the exponent of p in n's factorization.

title: The Function f(n)
content:
**logFloor(p, n)**: ⌊log_p(n)⌋ via Nat.log.

**primePowerBelow(p, n)**: p^⌊log_p(n)⌋, the largest power of p ≤ n.

**f(n)** = ∑_{p|n} primePowerBelow(p, n). The 'unconventional' part: ℓ depends on n globally.

**f_one**: f(1) = 0 (empty sum). **f_prime**: f(p) = p (axiomatized).
mathContext: Unlike standard additive functions where f(p^k) depends only on p and k, here the summand p^ℓ depends on n through ℓ = ⌊log_p n⌋. This makes the function harder to analyze.

title: The Function F(n)
content:
**ValidDecomposition(n)**: Pairwise coprime integers ≤ n whose prime factors divide n.

**F(n)** = sup over valid decompositions of sum of parts.

**f_le_F**: f(n) ≤ F(n) always (axiom). The prime-power decomposition {p^ℓ : p | n} is a valid decomposition, so f(n) is a lower bound for F(n).
mathContext: F(n) optimizes over all coprime representations. The gap between f and F reflects how much better optimal decompositions are compared to the canonical prime-power one.

title: The Four Open Questions
content:
**AlmostAll(P)**: Density of exceptions → 0.

**Question1_f/F**: Is f typically o(n log log n) while F is ≫ n log log n?

**Question2**: Is max_{n≤x} f(n) ~ x log x / log log x? (Finset.sup' with proper nonemptiness proof)

**Question3**: Do max f and max F coincide for large x?

All questions remain OPEN.
mathContext: The questions explore whether f and F behave differently 'typically' (almost all n) versus 'extremally' (maximum over n ≤ x). The Finset.sup' formulation avoids sorry by using range(x+1).

title: The Sum H(x) and No Mean Value
content:
**H(x)** = ∑_{n<x} f(n)/n.

**H_lower_bound**: H(x) ≥ c·x·log⁴x (4-fold iterated log).
**H_upper_bound**: H(x) ≤ C·x·log³x (3-fold iterated log).

**H_limsup_infinite**: limsup H(x)/x = ∞.
**H_liminf_finite**: liminf H(x)/x is finite.

**f_no_mean_value** (theorem): Combines both, showing f(n)/n has no mean value — very unusual for 'additive-like' functions.
mathContext: The lack of a mean value distinguishes f from conventional additive functions. The gap between 4-fold and 3-fold iterated logarithms in the H(x) bounds is also remarkable.

title: Erdős's 1984 Partial Asymptotic
content:
**erdos_1984**: There exists a strictly increasing sequence seq with seq → ∞ such that max_{n≤seq(k)} f(n) ~ seq(k)·log(seq(k))/log(log(seq(k))).

The asymptotic holds along SOME subsequence but not necessarily for ALL x. Whether it holds for all x is Question 2 (open).
mathContext: Erdős proved this in 1984. The subsequence restriction is significant — removing it is one of the main open questions.

title: Summary
content:
**erdos_878_summary** and **erdos_878**: Combine the known results:
1. f(n) ≤ F(n) for all n (f_le_F)
2. Erdős's bounds on H(x): x·log⁴x ≪ H(x) ≪ x·log³x
3. f(n)/n has no mean value (limsup = ∞, liminf finite)

Proved by combining f_le_F, H_lower_bound, H_upper_bound, and f_no_mean_value.

The main questions (Questions 1-3, precise H(x) asymptotic) remain OPEN.
mathContext: The summary captures what is known while the open questions are formalized as Prop definitions without being asserted.
